title: Redox Reactions
description: Oxidation and reduction as oxygen transfer and (Extended tier) electron transfer, Roman-numeral names, oxidation numbers, oxidising and reducing agents with the KMnO₄ and KI tests, and electrode half-equations for IGCSE Chemistry 0620.

notes.heading: Oxidation and Reduction: Oxygen Transfer
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
• **Oxidation** is the GAIN of oxygen by a substance.
• **Reduction** is the LOSS of oxygen from a substance.

🔑 Redox means both at once
A **redox reaction** is one in which oxidation and reduction happen SIMULTANEOUSLY — if one substance gains oxygen, another must lose it. The oxygen has to come from somewhere.

💡 Worked Example
CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O
• Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen → it is **reduced** to copper.
• Hydrogen gains oxygen → it is **oxidised** to water.
Both happen in the same reaction, so this is a redox reaction.

💡 Another Example
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO — magnesium gains oxygen, so it is oxidised to magnesium oxide.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Describing a reaction as 'just oxidation'. If magnesium is oxidised, the oxygen is reduced — name BOTH changes when the question asks about redox.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Oxidation = gain of O; reduction = loss of O.
• They always happen together — that is what 'redox' means.

notes.heading: Roman Numerals in Names
notes.body:
📌 What the numeral means
Some metals form ions with different charges. The Roman numeral in a name is the **oxidation number** of the metal in that compound:
• **iron(II)** compounds contain Fe²⁺ — e.g. iron(II) chloride, FeCl₂; iron(II) oxide, FeO.
• **iron(III)** compounds contain Fe³⁺ — e.g. iron(III) chloride, FeCl₃; iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃.
• **copper(II)** compounds contain Cu²⁺ — e.g. copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄.

🔑 How it works
The numeral tells you the charge on the metal ion, which lets you write the formula. Iron(III) oxide: Fe³⁺ pairs with O²⁻, and the charges balance as 2 × (+3) + 3 × (−2) = 0, giving Fe₂O₃.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reading the numeral as a NUMBER OF ATOMS. Iron(III) chloride is FeCl₃ not because of the (III) — the three chlorides come from balancing Fe³⁺ with three Cl⁻. The (III) describes the iron's oxidation number, and it happens that three Cl⁻ balance it.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• (II) = +2, (III) = +3 — the numeral is the metal ion's charge/oxidation number.
• Use the numeral + charge balance to build the formula.

notes.heading: Electron Transfer: OILRIG (Extended tier)
notes.body:
📌 Definitions (Extended tier)
• **Oxidation Is Loss** of electrons.
• **Reduction Is Gain** of electrons.
The mnemonic is **OILRIG**.

🔑 How it works
When magnesium reacts: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻. Magnesium LOSES two electrons, so it is oxidised. When copper(II) ions are displaced: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. The ions GAIN electrons, so they are reduced. The electrons lost by one species are gained by another — electron transfer is why oxidation and reduction always happen together.

💡 Worked Example
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
• Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (loss of electrons = oxidation)
• Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (gain of electrons = reduction)

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing the signs: electrons are NEGATIVE, so Losing the negative electrons makes a species MORE positive (Zn → Zn²⁺). If the charge goes up, electrons were lost — oxidation.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• OILRIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.
• Charge becoming more positive = oxidation; more negative/less positive = reduction.

notes.heading: Assigning Oxidation Numbers (Extended tier)
notes.body:
📌 The rules
1. An uncombined **element** has oxidation number **0** (Na, O₂, Cl₂).
2. In a compound or ion, the oxidation numbers **add up to the overall charge** (0 for a neutral compound).
3. **Oxygen** is usually **−2**.
4. **Hydrogen** is usually **+1**.
5. Group 1 metals are +1, Group 2 metals are +2 in compounds.

💡 Worked Examples
• Sulfur in SO₂: S + 2 × (−2) = 0, so S = **+4**.
• Nitrogen in NO₃⁻: N + 3 × (−2) = −1 (the ion's charge), so N = **+5**.
• Chlorine in ClO⁻: Cl + (−2) = −1, so Cl = **+1**.

🔑 Why it matters
Oxidation numbers tell you what is oxidised and what is reduced WITHOUT needing electron bookkeeping:
• oxidation number **increases** → the species has been **oxidised**;
• oxidation number **decreases** → the species has been **reduced**.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting rule 2 for IONS: the numbers sum to the ion's charge, not zero. In NO₃⁻ the sum is −1, which is why N = +5 and not +6.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Element = 0; sum = overall charge; O = −2; H = +1.
• Rise = oxidation; fall = reduction.

notes.heading: Oxidising and Reducing Agents (Extended tier)
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
• An **oxidising agent** oxidises another substance — and is itself REDUCED in the process.
• A **reducing agent** reduces another substance — and is itself OXIDISED.

🔑 The two colour-change tests you must know
1. **Acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄** — deep PURPLE solution. If a substance turns it **colourless**, the substance is a **reducing agent** (it reduces the manganate(VII)).
2. **Potassium iodide, KI** — colourless solution. If a substance turns it **brown** (iodine, I₂, is formed), the substance is an **oxidising agent** (it oxidises I⁻ to I₂).

💡 Worked Example
Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂: the colourless solution turns brown. Chlorine oxidises I⁻ to I₂, so chlorine is the oxidising agent — and Cl₂ (oxidation number 0) is itself reduced to Cl⁻ (−1).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Naming the agent by what happens to IT. Name it by what it DOES to the other substance: the oxidising agent is the one that gets reduced.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• KMnO₄ purple → colourless = reducing agent present.
• KI colourless → brown = oxidising agent present.
• The agent is itself changed in the OPPOSITE way to its name.

notes.heading: Half-Equations at Electrodes (Extended tier)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A **half-equation** shows what happens at ONE electrode (or to ONE species), with electrons written in explicitly. The electrolysis topic gives you the products; here you write how they form.

🔑 The method
1. Write the species before and after (atoms balanced).
2. Balance the CHARGE by adding electrons (e⁻) to the more positive side.

💡 Worked Examples
• **Cathode (reduction — gain of electrons):** Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Check the charge: left side +2 − 2 = 0, right side 0 ✓.
• **Cathode:** 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ ✓.
• **Anode (oxidation — loss of electrons):** 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Charge: left −2, right −2 ✓.
• **Anode:** 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ ✓.

🔑 Link to the electrodes
Reduction (gain of electrons) always happens at the **cathode**; oxidation (loss of electrons) at the **anode**.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Electrons on the wrong side. Gained electrons go on the LEFT (with the reactant); lost electrons go on the RIGHT (as a product). Then check that the total charge balances on both sides.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Balance atoms first, then charge with e⁻.
• Cathode = reduction; anode = oxidation.

notes.heading: Spotting Redox in the Exam
notes.body:
0620 loves an 'explain why this is a redox reaction' question. This is the reliable method.

🔑 The method
1. Assign oxidation numbers to the key elements on BOTH sides.
2. Look for a species whose number RISES (oxidised) and one whose number FALLS (reduced).
3. State both changes — that pairing is what makes it redox.

💡 Worked Example
Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
• Zn: 0 → +2 — oxidation number rises, zinc is **oxidised** (loses electrons).
• Cu: +2 → 0 — oxidation number falls, copper(II) ions are **reduced** (gain electrons).
• Zinc is the reducing agent; Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent.

🔑 Where redox appears
• **Rusting:** iron is oxidised (0 → +3 in Fe₂O₃).
• **Displacement:** the more reactive metal is oxidised.
• **Metal extraction:** the metal oxide is reduced to the metal.
• **Electrolysis:** reduction at the cathode, oxidation at the anode.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Answering 'in terms of electron transfer' with an oxygen-transfer answer (or vice versa). Read the command words: 'in terms of electrons' needs gain/loss of e⁻; 'in terms of oxidation number' needs the numbers quoted.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Quote the oxidation-number change OR the electron transfer — whichever the question asks for.
• Always name both the oxidised and the reduced species.

flashcards.definition: The gain of oxygen by a substance.
The loss of oxygen from a substance.
flashcards.example: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O: copper(II) oxide is reduced to copper.

flashcards.definition: A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen simultaneously — one species is oxidised while another is reduced.
flashcards.example: Zn + CuO → ZnO + Cu: zinc is oxidised and copper(II) oxide is reduced.

flashcards.definition: The oxidation number (charge) of the metal ion in the compound: iron(II) = Fe²⁺, iron(III) = Fe³⁺, copper(II) = Cu²⁺.
flashcards.example: Iron(III) chloride is FeCl₃; iron(II) chloride is FeCl₂.

flashcards.definition: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons (Extended).
flashcards.example: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ is oxidation; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu is reduction.

flashcards.definition: Uncombined element = 0; the numbers in a species sum to its overall charge; oxygen is usually −2 and hydrogen +1 (Extended).
flashcards.example: In SO₂: S + 2(−2) = 0, so sulfur is +4.

flashcards.definition: A substance that oxidises another substance and is itself reduced (Extended).
flashcards.example: Cl₂ is the oxidising agent in Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂.

flashcards.definition: A substance that reduces another substance and is itself oxidised (Extended).
flashcards.example: Zn is the reducing agent in Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.

flashcards.definition: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) is purple; it turns colourless in the presence of a reducing agent (Extended).
flashcards.example: Purple → colourless shows the added substance is a reducing agent.

flashcards.definition: Colourless potassium iodide solution turns brown (iodine forms) in the presence of an oxidising agent (Extended).
flashcards.example: Colourless → brown shows the added substance is an oxidising agent.

flashcards.definition: An equation for one electrode process with electrons shown explicitly; balance atoms, then balance charge with e⁻ (Extended).
Reduction (gain of electrons) always happens at the cathode; oxidation (loss of electrons) at the anode (Extended).
flashcards.example: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ is the cathode half-equation in the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid.

questions.stem: In terms of oxygen transfer, what is oxidation?
choices: The gain of oxygen by a substance
The loss of oxygen from a substance
The breakdown of a compound by heat
questions.explanation: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen; reduction is the loss of oxygen. The two always happen together in a redox reaction.

questions.stem: What does the (III) in the name iron(III) chloride tell you?
choices: The formula contains three iron atoms
The iron has oxidation number +3 (Fe³⁺ ions)
The compound contains exactly three chloride ions per formula unit
The iron has gained three oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: The Roman numeral is the metal's oxidation number — iron(III) means Fe³⁺. The formula FeCl₃ follows from balancing Fe³⁺ with three Cl⁻; the numeral itself describes the iron, not the atom count.

questions.stem: In the reaction Mg + CuO → MgO + Cu, which substance is oxidised?
choices: Copper(II) oxide, because it contains oxygen
Copper, because it is a product
No substance — this is not a redox reaction
questions.explanation: Magnesium gains oxygen to become MgO, so magnesium is oxidised. Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen to become Cu, so it is reduced — oxidation and reduction happen together.

questions.stem: In terms of electron transfer (Extended tier), oxidation is:
questions.explanation: OILRIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons. Gain of oxygen is the Core definition of oxidation, not the electron-transfer one.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in SO₂? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: Oxygen is −2 and the molecule is neutral, so S + 2 × (−2) = 0, giving S = +4. +6 is sulfur's oxidation number in SO₃ or SO₄²⁻.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: The oxidation numbers must sum to the ion's charge, −1: N + 3 × (−2) = −1, so N = +5. Summing to zero instead of −1 wrongly gives +6.

questions.stem: In Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which species is the reducing agent? (Extended tier)
choices: Cu, because it is the metal product
Zn, because it loses electrons and reduces Cu²⁺
Zn²⁺, because its charge is higher
questions.explanation: The reducing agent reduces the OTHER species and is itself oxidised. Zn goes from oxidation number 0 to +2 — it loses electrons (is oxidised) and reduces Cu²⁺ to Cu. Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: A colourless solution turns acidified potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless. What does this show? (Extended tier)
choices: The solution contains an oxidising agent
The solution contains a transition-metal compound
The solution contains a reducing agent
questions.explanation: Purple acidified KMnO₄ is decolourised when it is reduced, so the added solution must be a reducing agent. The reverse test — KI turning brown — detects an oxidising agent.

questions.stem: What is the formula of iron(III) oxide?
questions.explanation: Iron(III) means Fe³⁺, and oxide is O²⁻. Balancing charges: 2 × (+3) + 3 × (−2) = 0, so the formula is Fe₂O₃. FeO is iron(II) oxide.

questions.stem: What is observed when an oxidising agent is added to colourless potassium iodide solution? (Extended tier)
choices: The solution turns brown as iodine forms
questions.explanation: An oxidising agent oxidises iodide ions to iodine (2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻), and the iodine colours the solution brown. Purple → colourless is the KMnO₄ test for a REDUCING agent — do not mix the two up.

questions.stem: Which is the correct half-equation for the reduction of iron(III) ions to iron(II) ions at a cathode? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: Reduction is GAIN of electrons, so e⁻ appears on the left with the reactant: Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺. Check: atoms balance (1 Fe each side) and charge balances (+3 − 1 = +2 on both sides). The other options either put electrons on the wrong side or fail to balance charge.

questions.stem: During electrolysis, the process at the cathode is always: (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: The cathode is the negative electrode, so positive ions arrive there and GAIN electrons — gain of electrons is reduction (OILRIG). Oxidation happens at the anode.

questions.stem: Chlorine reacts with potassium iodide: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂. Which species is the oxidising agent? (Extended tier)
choices: Cl₂ — it oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and is itself reduced to Cl⁻
KI — because it contains the iodine
KCl — because it is the salt product
I₂ — because it is the coloured product
questions.explanation: Chlorine takes electrons from the iodide ions (2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻), so it oxidises them; chlorine's own oxidation number falls from 0 to −1, so it is reduced. The agent that does the oxidising — Cl₂ — is the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of chlorine in the hypochlorite ion, ClO⁻? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: The numbers sum to the ion's charge: Cl + (−2) = −1, so Cl = +1. The familiar −1 is chlorine's oxidation number in chloride ions such as Cl⁻ — in ClO⁻ the oxygen 'uses up' the −2.

questions.stem: Iron(II) ions react with chlorine: 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻. Which statement is correct? (Extended tier)
choices: Fe²⁺ is oxidised — its oxidation number rises from +2 to +3
The oxidation number of chlorine rises from 0 to −1
questions.explanation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ is a rise in oxidation number (+2 to +3) — loss of an electron — so iron(II) is oxidised. Chlorine falls from 0 to −1, so Cl₂ is reduced. Note that a fall to −1 is a DECREASE, so the last option misreads the sign.
